profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research lab between the project lead and the primary implementer for a workshop paper extension on theory-driven one-shot topology generation. They are preparing a two-week execution plan to produce the next internal milestone: a reproducible experiment package and a draft set of figures showing that the theory-driven student-teacher loop improves generalization under a fixed compute budget on compliance minimization tasks. The agenda is to decide what exactly will be included in the milestone, how the new experiment batch will be run, how results will be summarized, and who owns each piece. The expected outcome is an aligned plan for experiments, analysis, and timeline for a lab review next Friday.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: Scientific machine learning, topology optimization, ML-for-physics benchmarking
members.background: Leads a university ML research group and previously published on physics-guided learning for inverse design; she usually thinks in terms of paper narratives, benchmark comparability, and review-ready evidence.
members.private_state: She wants the milestone to support a compelling paper story for the workshop submission and is worried about overcommitting the team to extra infrastructure work that does not directly improve the figures.
hidden_assumptions: A 'reproducible package' for an internal milestone means a clean code snapshot plus a fixed seed setup that another lab member can rerun later, not a containerized end-to-end artifact.
When people refer to the 'budget-matched comparison,' they naturally mean matching the number of expensive teacher calls because that is the scarce resource in theory-driven learning.
A 'generalization plot' should aggregate performance over the full unseen test suite into a single main curve suitable for the paper, with subgroup breakdowns as optional appendix material.

Using the 'same benchmark as last time' means the canonical cantilever compliance setup from their previous internal report, including the standard 64x64 resolution and the usual boundary-condition family.

members.name: Ethan Morales
members.expertise: Deep learning systems, experiment pipelines, differentiable mechanics implementations
members.background: He built the current training codebase and maintains the lab's experiment tracking; he tends to think operationally about reruns, scripts, and ablation hygiene.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid another rushed milestone with ambiguous handoff requirements, and is trying to steer the plan toward robust experiment packaging and diagnostics that will save time later.
hidden_assumptions: A 'reproducible package' means anyone in the lab should be able to rerun the exact milestone results from scratch on a fresh machine using the standard container and job scripts.
A 'budget-matched comparison' should match total wall-clock GPU-hours because that is the fairest practical resource accounting for the overall method.
A 'generalization plot' should include per-load-case or per-boundary-condition breakdowns, because aggregate means can hide systematic failure modes that matter for debugging.

The 'same benchmark as last time' refers to the current codebase's default benchmark bundle, which expanded after the last internal report to include both cantilever and simply supported beam variants at 128x128.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the reproducible package
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to deliver a 'reproducible package' for the lab review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a tidy repository snapshot, saved configs, and fixed random seeds sufficient for a lab member to rerun core experiments with some manual setup later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a containerized, script-driven artifact that recreates the exact tables and plots end-to-end on a fresh environment with minimal manual intervention.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are experienced researchers who routinely use 'reproducible package' as a positive, familiar term, and each assumes the lab's norms are obvious; because they are only planning an internal milestone, neither expects the other to need the phrase unpacked.

misalignment_points.topic: How the budget-matched comparison is matched
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the new results should be 'budget-matched' against the supervised baseline.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the comparison is fair if the theory-driven and supervised methods use the same number of teacher optimization solves or queried training additions, since those dominate scientific novelty and data efficiency claims.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the comparison is fair if both methods consume roughly the same total GPU-hours and end-to-end training time, regardless of how many teacher solves were involved.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They already agree on the high-level fairness goal and have discussed budget constraints many times, so the phrase sounds sufficiently precise; the differing fairness criteria are second-order and would only matter later when they tabulate runs.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'use the same benchmark as last time' for the milestone.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the benchmark from the previous internal report: cantilever compliance only, 64x64 grid, with the standard load/support distribution used in the draft figures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the benchmark bundle currently labeled 'default' in the codebase: cantilever plus simply supported beam cases at 128x128, introduced after that report.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both can sincerely refer to a shared past benchmark without noticing they anchor to different artifacts: M1 to the prior report and M2 to the updated pipeline defaults; the phrase sounds like routine continuity rather than a decision point.

misalignment_points.topic: What the generalization plot should include
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to prepare a 'generalization plot' for unseen problems.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects one main aggregate plot over all unseen problems, suitable for the paper's central claim, with maybe a short note if some subgroups differ.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the deliverable to include stratified plots by boundary-condition family and load regime in addition to the aggregate, because otherwise the plot is not informative enough for diagnosing one-shot failure modes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both view subgroup analysis as obviously compatible with a generalization plot, but differ on whether it is inside or outside the default scope; because the phrase is common and underspecified, the boundary mismatch feels too minor to clarify during planning.

turns.inner_thought: For next Friday I need something that reads like a clean milestone, not a sprawling engineering sprint. The core is a convincing workshop story extension: teacher-guided one-shot generation improves outcomes on unseen compliance problems. A reproducible package, for this review, just needs to be a tidy code snapshot with the right configs, seeds, and notes so someone in the group can rerun the main experiments later. I do not want us burning the week on infrastructure work that won't show up in the figures.
turns.utterance: Okay, let’s keep this tight. By next Friday I want a clean internal milestone: a reproducible package, plus a small set of figures that extends the theory-driven one-shot topology story in a way we can actually discuss at lab review.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I need the handoff to be unambiguous this time. If we call it a reproducible package, I want it to actually rerun from scratch in the standard container with the usual scripts. For the experiments, using the same benchmark as last time should keep things sane since the codebase default bundle is already wired up and tested: cantilever plus simply supported beam at 128x128. That should make the reruns and comparisons straightforward.
turns.utterance: That works. I can base the plan on the same benchmark as last time so the reruns and comparisons stay straightforward, and then build the milestone around that.

turns.inner_thought: The headline result has to be a budget-matched comparison where the adaptive teacher loop beats the supervised baseline under the same teacher-query budget. That is the fairness criterion that matters for the scientific claim. And for the paper-facing story, the generalization plot should be one clear main curve over the full unseen suite. If there are subgroup quirks, those can live in backup material.
turns.utterance: Right. The key result for me is a budget-matched comparison against the supervised baseline, showing better generalization under the same compute envelope. If we have that and a clear generalization plot for unseen problems, the review will have something concrete to react to.

turns.inner_thought: If we're calling it budget-matched, I should make the accounting explicit in the logs so I can line up total runtime and GPU-hours between methods. Otherwise we'll end up arguing about fairness after the fact. I should front-load the runs Monday and Tuesday, because if anything drifts in the pipeline I still have time to patch it.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I’ll schedule the main runs early in the week and track total runtime carefully as they go, so the budget-matched table is easy to assemble instead of being reconstructed at the end.

turns.inner_thought: He can sort out the bookkeeping however he likes, but what I need first is the figure that tells us whether the method has a paper-worthy signal. The generalization plot is the decision point. If that aggregate curve looks good, I can build the narrative around it quickly.
turns.utterance: Good. I’d prioritize the generalization plot first, though, because that’s probably what everyone will look at to decide whether the teacher-guided sampling is genuinely helping on unseen problems.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. But I don't want another misleading average hiding a bad failure mode. The generalization plot should include the breakdowns by condition family and load regime so we can see whether one subset is collapsing. I can still give her the aggregate view, but to me the informative version includes the stratified diagnostics.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that’s the right first readout. I’ll break out the unseen cases by condition family as well, so the generalization plot is still informative if one regime behaves differently from the others.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, extra breakdowns are harmless as long as they don’t derail the main figure. The budget-matched comparison itself should be reported at the same acquisition milestones for the adaptive teacher loop and the supervised learner, since matching teacher calls is the fair comparison. That’s the cleanest way to support the data-efficiency claim.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. And for the budget-matched comparison, I mainly want the adaptive teacher loop and the supervised learner evaluated at the same acquisition milestones, so the comparison reads cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: Using the default benchmark configuration should let me launch everything without custom branching, and if I push it all through the existing experiment container then the artifact will be rerunnable by anyone in the lab. That's exactly the kind of reproducible package I want us to normalize. It will take some setup, but it'll save time later.
turns.utterance: That should fit. I can reuse the default benchmark configuration and launch everything through the existing experiment container, which should keep the run management pretty clean.

turns.inner_thought: Great, as long as he’s not turning this into a week-long packaging exercise. For the review, the reproducible package can just travel with the figures and notes so another student can revisit it later. I mainly care that the setup is tidy and recoverable, not polished like a public artifact.
turns.utterance: Great. Then the reproducible package can just accompany the figures and the draft notes, so another student can revisit the setup later if needed.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—that gives me room to make it actually usable. I'll wire the training reruns and figure generation into one path and hand the lab a single command. If this is going to be called reproducible, I want fresh-machine reproducibility, not a folder of checkpoints and best-effort notes.
